David Smith

David Smith

David Smith  

This book is the most succinct and up-to-date account of the Communicative Approach to psychoanalytic psychotherapy available in print. Beginning with The Bipersonal Field (1976) Langs has gradually developed a radical and distinctive alternative to existing forms of psychoanalysis. Although originally inspired by the early Freud, Searles, Bion and Little, to name but a few, the Communicative Approach has developed to the point of being relatively independent of its sources.

Langs' work stems from the fundamental proposition that the unconscious part of the mind is basically an organ of interpersonal perception, as opposed to the autistic phantasy-ridden system dominated by the pleasure principle described by other writers. Langs shows that what he calls the deep unconscious system is much more sensitive in this respect than the conscious mind. Unconscious perceptions attach themselves to preconscious thoughts to produce disguised derivatives, much in the way that Freud describes in The Interpretation of Dreams.

This approach to the unconscious mind has radical implications for therapeutic technique. The patient is seen as constantly unconsciously monitoring the therapist's behaviour and feeding back his or her observations in derivative form. The technique that Langs has developed, then, is based on learning to understand these messages and to let the patient teach one how to conduct the therapy. When listening to patients in this way some surprising and often unsettling results emerge. Many conventional psychoanalytic methods (such as interpreting ‘transference’) are not unconsciously ‘validated’. Many of these methods are unconsciously experienced by patients as acts of violence, seduction or deception.

Matte-Blanco started developing his ideas more than 40 years ago as can be seen by reviewing the reference list at the end of the book. It was my privilege to have met Matte-Blanco 35 years ago and to have worked with him during the first years in which he formulated the basic thoughts of what today constitutes the main body of his theories, that is, the concepts of symmetry and asymmetry, of bi-logic and of the fundamental antinomy.

Matte-Blanco writes in a systematic way which shows him in his lifelong role as an exponent and teacher of Psychoanalysis. The book has 5 parts and 16 chapters divided in numerous sub-chapters plus 32 clinical examples. For the non-initiated there is a very useful introduction by Eric Rayner and David Tuckett. For the mathematically shy and fearful there is just the indispensable higher calculus and geometry in order to understand some of the scientific points which reaffirm the clinical-theoretical issues presented here. Matte-Blanco takes the reader through an amazing amount of analytical theory and practice explaining it in the light of bi-logic. In this way we are given a tour de force through Freud's postulations about the Unconscious, projection, introjection and dreams. Matte-Blanco revises Freud's conception of the Unconscious in detail and shows how Freud had the geniality of intuiting the logical laws which govern the Unconscious, the facts of timelessness and spacelessness and what Freud explained as telescoping and substituting which Matte-Blanco sees as the whole represented by any of its parts and vice versa, any part represented by the whole. Chapter 6 of the Interpretations of Dreams is quoted at large to show these facts. The Schreber case is used to explain some of the basic Freudian ideas about internal and external world. Here Matte-Blanco starts to develop and analyse the conceptual problem of inside-outside as a psychological formulation in contrast to physical reality. He then goes into developing the problem of psychological space and its dimensions.

Mother, Madonna, Whore: the Idealisation and Denigration of Motherhood by Estela V. Welldon. Published by Free Association Books, 1988.

Nina Coltart

Nina Coltart

Nina Coltart  

In this readable book Estela Welldon holds our attention by her clinical experience, deployed skilfully to demonstrate the creative views which she has developed from it. She shows her respect for the Freudian and Kleinian traditions, and her divergences from them, derived from her long treatments of perversions presenting in women. ‘Women can't have perversions because they haven't got a penis’ is one of the shibboleths she accurately dismantles, and along with it, some of its lesser, but Sacred, Cows. Welldon satisfactorily demythologises several Sacred Cows; in fact the intention to do so is implicit in the book's arresting title.

For too long, certain concepts were handed on from one generation to the next in our field, enshrined as idées reçues. Only men have perversions; perversions arise in a (failed) Oedipal stage of development; the baby is a woman's ‘second-best’ achievement, a substitute for the penis; child sexual abuse is the province of men, where it occasionally exists; many female patients' accounts of sexual seduction in childhood are fantasies (the subject of one of the latest passionate debates, especially as to its origins). the Breast is always symbolic of the whole mother - many workers in our whole field of dynamic psychology will have no difficulty in recognising this herd of Sacred Cows. Welldon persists reflectively in developing her own structure of thought beyond these developmental stages in the history of psychoanalysis, without excessive provocation and without wasting energy on too much confrontational argument. This is not to say that all her ideas are original nor that she claims originality where there is already in existence parallel or convergent work from others; she acknowledges and uses this fully as she proceeds, and it is the richness of her clinical experience which brings her own authenticity to the form and content of her book.

She extends the boundaries of the study of the psychology of the Self beyond the limitations of both Freudian and Kleinian theory. Freudian theory is phallocentric, and both men and women are viewed as on the same developmental spectrum towards genitality, and woman is seen primarily as the being-without-a-Penis. Kleinian theory re-focuses on the Mother, herself constricted to repetitive representation by the Breast - goodness and badness emanate from the infant and fill the Breast; the fundamental idée reçue being that, other things being equal, the Breast is good-in-itself. In both traditions, it can be argued that scant importance is attached to the environment since in both various innate driven characteristics in the infant predominate, and there is little true context for the almost infinite complexity of the interactions between two radically different sexes. Welldon is more conditioned by Kleinian views but they do not rule her thinking, and she clearly emphasises early in the book that while Freudian theory is about male sex, Kleinian is about feeding or what is, in passing, referred to as ‘the mammalian ecological function’; both views carry severe inherent limitations, which too often have not been questioned. Welldon is concerned with the profound differences between the psychic structures, and the self-representations, of the sexes, with her particular focus reserved for the power and influence, especially for ill, of the (more secret) self of the mother. She shows what it is like to have different types of mother, especially as a girl-child, what it is like to become, and be, a mother, with the effects of that childhood built into the system, where the conscious and unconscious of the mother are internalised, themselves moulded by the same process … and so ad infinitum.

This paper presents the rationale for a brief form of psychotherapy based on the Conversational Model of psychotherapy developed by R F Hobson. In the proposed model, termed Two-Plus-One Exploratory therapy, clients are seen for two sessions one week apart followed by a third session three months later. [[RunningHead]]

Gender Identity - Fifty Years on from Freud

Margot Waddell

Margot Waddell

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Margot Waddell  

The issue of gender identity confronts us with the problem of self-knowledge - how we may understand the landscape of our souls. The psychoanalytic process allows insight into the fundamental distinction between the secrets of femininity or masculinity, of womanhood or manhood in their descriptive and socially available attributes, and their mysteries, in terms of the internal meanings. The distinction denotes different modes of thought, different mentalities, related to the geography of mental spaces and the relationships between them. It can roughly be designated as that between intrusive or voyeuristic curiosity on the one hand, and a thirst for knowledge, knowledge that is of the inner self, on the other: between the superficial contours without and the unmapped country within.

These discriminations are rooted in different kinds of identification process, the nature and functioning of which have preoccupied, indeed almost characterised, psychoanalytic thinking during the last fifty years. This relationship between secrets and mysteries and their penumbra of meanings has also, as Meg Harris Williams has pointed out, been ‘continuously analysed and exorcised by creative writers. Shakespeare dramatised it through Polonius, who sets off to “find/Where truth is hid, though it were hid indeed/Within the centre” and Hamlet condemns the hermetic procedures of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern who try to “pluck out the heart of my mystery”. Milton imaged it in the little devils who “Rifled the bowels of their mother earth/For treasures better hid”’ (1986).

As a mode of denying mental pain and avoiding real experience, this desire to discover the secrets rather than to endure and explore the mysteries is, as Mrs Harris Williams puts it, ‘an eternal aspect of the human condition’. George Eliot, in the short story The Lifted Veil, describes the same phenomenon in the central character, Latimer's intrusion into the mental world of others through his strange powers of prescience and super-added consciousness. Latimer mistakes accuracy of external representation for reality. His reality, however, is wholly devoid of the poetry of inner experience based, as that is, in the hard, internal work through which images become imbued with meaning - meaning culled from ‘the vale of soul making’ (Keats).

[[RunningHead]]

The Arrival of the Bee Box: Poetry and Mental Mechanism

Melanie Hart

Melanie Hart

13 Sibella Road, London SW4

Melanie Hart  

In Jeremy Holmes's interesting paper ‘The language of psychotherapy: metaphor, ambiguity and wholeness’ (Holmes 1985) he illustrates the characteristics of analytic language by comparing poetry and psychoanalysis. The context of his discussion is the view … ‘that psychoanalysis, whatever its scientific aspirations, is fundamentally a linguistic or interpretive discipline, primarily concerned with meaning rather than mechanism’. He suggests further that ‘… metaphor, standing transitionally (Winnicott 1971) between the entirely unspoken private thought and the generalisation, is poetic and analytic truth. … A consequence of this viewpoint is that analytic theory becomes not so much a body of objective knowledge as a set of rules and guidelines for interpreting transferential metaphors … theory is a language for describing the experience of therapy’.

Considering these ideas in relation to my work with a very disturbed young patient, I wondered whether it might be possible, through an interpretation of metaphor, to locate in certain sorts of poetry some of the mental mechanisms described in analytic theory which seemed relevant to her way of being. Those that interested me are central to the hypotheses about mental functioning in the paranoid-schizoid position and manic depression put forward by Melanie Klein (Klein, from 1935 onwards) and Wilfred Bion's amplification of these. In particular, I was interested to explore Bion's observations of psychotic processes, especially his descriptions, so difficult to grasp, of the vicissitudes of the senses and of verbal thought (mutilation, compression and agglomeration) under the impact of projective identification (Bion 1956, 1957 and elsewhere), and the notion of the need for containment. Since the writing of poetry presupposes at the very least a facility for verbal thought, I was not very sanguine about this enterprise. However, knowledge of Sylvia Plath's biography prompted the idea that such theoretical reference points might be recognisable in her work. I could not guess at the way in which they seem to me to illuminate each other. The poem I have chosen was written towards the end of her life and is called The Arrival of the Bee Box.

New Ideas about the Unconscious Family Structure

Isidoro Berenstein

Isidoro Berenstein

Republica de la India 2921, 9'A', (1425) Buenos Aires, Argentina

Isidoro Berenstein  

Unconscious Family Structure (UFS) is the virtual, symbolic space, the deep level level where lies the meaning which organises the family relations or the manifest level. Within the UFS space there are subspaces: that of the marital couple, later to become the parents, that of the children in relation to the parents, that of the children in relation to each other. Within these subspaces certain places are to be found: the father's place, the mother's place and the child's place. Between the spaces lie the relationships or links: the couple or marital link; the filial link between parents and their children; the consanguineous link between siblings. To these I add a fourth: the avunculus link with the representative of the mother's family.

I depict a series of verbal or preverbal stipulations: the unconscious accords, pacts and rules.

In addition I describe four UFS configurations: grade a (‘normal’), b (‘neurotic’), c ‘perverse’) and d (‘psychotic’).

I conclude with some observations about family transference and countertransference.

Once upon A Time the Infant in the Lacanian Theory

Bice Benvenuto

Bice Benvenuto

23 Primrose Gardens, London NW3

Bice Benvenuto  

By setting up a dialogue with the ‘adult’ unconscious of his patients, Freud had to admit, not without scandal for those times, that he was inevitably led into the dark area of childhood sexuality.

That the child is the father of the man, as E Armstrong-Perlman reminded us in her introduction to this series of articles on infant development, is a truth which only became so in our culture, more precisely, from the time that psychoanalysis discovered the importance of childhood for the unconscious of adult patients. Thanks to this discovery the child has become the centre of interest in most branches of our culture and understanding in a way as never before in history, as the historian Philippe Aries suggests in his interesting book on the history of the family in the Ancien Regime.'

Childhood seems to contain in itself the mystery of our origin. It is the foundation for any further development. That the quest for the mystery of origins holds strong in psychoanalysis can be seen in the way it traces man's relation to the world further and further back, into the mists of an original state, as if to catch it in the act, at its birth. Like story-tellers, psychoanalysts too would like to start the story with a ‘Once upon a time’.

Like the cell in biology and the atom in physics, psychoanalysis too looks for the irreducible unit of the psychic world. Object relation theory, in spite of all its variations of emphases, postulates the irreducible relation to a primary object (namely, the breast) which will determine to a greater or lesser extent the internal world of the infant and thus, eventually, the adult. As for the nature of this object there are different emphases according to different schools, whether it is an external or an internal object or in which way phantasy and external reality interact in the constitution of the psychic object.

Generally the advocates of this original unit, which is specifically the mother-child one, reproach Freud for not having gone further with the reconstruction of childhood in analysis, implying that if he had done so he would inevitably have realised the importance of earlier and earlier stages of development. But such a reproach does not take into account that the one they reproach for such a lacuna is the very discoverer of psychic infantile development, and his developmental pre-oedipal stages and their fundamental importance in our sexual choice are still the unchallenged milestones on which all later work on infancy is based.

A Secure Base is a collection of lectures given by Dr John Bowlby since 1979 on various aspects of Attachment theory. In his Preface he expresses his disappointment that, while his theories have inspired a large number of investigations in developmental psychology, clinicians ‘have been so slow to test the theory's uses’. He believes this may be due to a ‘reluctance to spend time trying to master a new and strange conceptual framework’ and he hopes these lectures may represent a ‘convenient introduction’ for those who have decided to spend some time discovering what his theories have to offer. Indeed, this book is a detailed, lucid and rich statement of Dr Bowlby's theory and I hope it will be read with the care and attention it deserves.

Bowlby sees his work as developing ‘out of the object-relations tradition in psychoanalysis; but it has drawn also on concepts from evolution theory, ethology, control theory and cognitive psychology’ (p. 120). Bowlby refers (p. 43) to the climate prevailing in the British Psychoanalytical Society when he qualified in 1937, when ‘it was regarded as almost outside the proper interest of an analyst to give systematic attention to a person's real experiences’. ‘To me as a biologist this contrast of internal with external, of organism with environment, never appealed’ and he goes onto quote examples of cases where the children's behaviour was clearly linked to childhood experiences of their parents. From these findings Bowlby came to choose his field of observation and embarked on the research that made him a world famous name.

Anton Obholzer  

Isabel Menzies Lyth is this generation's best known writer on psychoanalytic perspectives on caring institutions - this book makes it clear what the basis of her reputation is, and why it is deservedly so. The book, the first of a two-volume compendium of her writings, contains some of her best papers, ‘The functioning of social systems as a defence against anxiety’ (1959), two papers on ‘Action research in a

461

long stay hospital’ (1973, 1982), ‘Staff support systems: task and anti-task in adolescent institutions’ (1979), and ‘The development of the self in children in institutions’ (1985). Some of these papers have been added to/modified since the original publications. Additional social perspective is added by the inclusion in the volume of letters in response to the early nursing paper. Also included is her paper ‘Thoughts on the maternal role in contemporary society’ (1975) and a 42-page interview with the author entitled ‘Reflections on my work’.

The volume hangs together well. Robert Young who commissioned the volume and Ann Scott, the Editor, are to be congratulated on making this important body of work available to the professional public.

The earliest paper, the study of the nursing service of a general hospital, is as relevant as ever. In it she spells out the pain inherent in the work, the defences against the anxiety, and how these anti-task phenomena are presented as if they were the most task appropriate way of organising the work. In spite of now being 30 years old, it is probably still the best paper in the field of applying psycho-analytical concepts to the understanding of an institution.

The two papers, ‘Action research in a long stay hospital’, are preceded by a most useful paper, ‘Some methodological notes on a hospital study’. This excellent precursor to the hospital study gives a detailed account of theoretical and technical issues which need to be considered prior to embarking on an institutional consultation. Together, the three papers give a comprehensive picture of the fundamental principles of the action-research method as pioneered at the Tavistock Institute of Human Relations in their application of psychoanalytic insights in work with institutions.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Following on from two papers in the last issue on the limits of psychotherapy, in this issue we publish two papers, by Mike Power and by Peter Fonagy, forming a section on the relations between psycho-analytic psychotherapy and cognitive therapy. One a cognitive therapist and one a psycho-analyst, they achieve a considerable degree of agreement! If one concedes that cognitive therapy lacks a good theory of aetiology or causation, the other acknowledges that elements of practice, suspiciously like cognitive therapy, seem to creep into the work of a practising psycho-analyst. This is an honourable co-operativeness. Nilman and Lewin also describe a combining of techniques in their successful treatment of a latency age child. Using dramatic techniques with a boy who had lost a needed object, they were able to restore his ‘whole object capacity’ to love. The problem is: how does such a mixture work, how does it effect the patient if contrasting styles, ideas lie side by side.

Adding to the hopeful atmosphere of integration in Psychotherapy, is the reminder of the developments at ‘Rugby’ (wherever it is) in Mike Pokorny's address from the Chair at last January's Conference. Though rumblings from the Conference echo in the Correspondence section.

How to use the material is a question asked by Nathan Field in attending to the responses he gets from his body. One might wonder if in fact the body, in spite of all the medical knowledge of physiology, functions much more mysteriously for each individual even than his own mind. Perhaps it seems so for those with serious and long-term pathology like the diabetics treated by Jane Milton, who are daily presented with their wayward bodily functions. It is that border land period of development, when the infant is sorting out that basic space-time framework which our minds use, that Andrea Sabbadini focusses in on. He states the classical framework for thinking about the development of that mental framework, and uses it to study how development does and does not work.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

The peculiarly unreachable area of the body-mind boundary is the topic of two papers in this issue. Robin Royston tackles the disputed territory of the causation of schizophrenia. He joins the recent trend towards finding common ground between the biological genetics and the psychological factors. He finds the unifying factor in Jung's archetypes, and Jung's ideas on the relation between the unconscious and physiological processes.

In an intriguing contrast Dennis Brown's paper includes the social aspect of human beings. If they are bio-psycho-social entities he postulates the arresting idea that it is the social aspect that can most enlighten the mysteries of the boundary between the biological and the psychic. If that boundary is one which has to be crossed by a movement from non-symbolic to symbolic forms of communication, then it is the entry of the human being into the social world that drives the transition from biological to psychological being. So what is the proper image of man? Psycho-somatic or biopsycho-social? Jonathan Pedder explores a series of much more poetic images of mankind, particularly the centaur. And Hazel Guest charts the historical progress in psychotherapy from behavioural to psychoanalytic, to humanistic and eventually towards claiming a spiritual dimension as a key element in psychotherapy. This fourth force, transpersonal psychology, she describes as reaching beyond the humanism of humanistic psychology to a higher spiritual domain.

Gail Yariv reflects in her paper on the very fundamental place that respect for, or violation of, boundaries has in human experiences. Her essay reviews the psychological level of this essential developmental step that is so close to the physical properties of the human body. In a related vein the experience of the other person as a subject who also experiences, and the boundary with them has led Robert Hobson to develop his conversational model of psychotherapy; and Michael Barkham has extended this model to a form of brief psychotherapy which he describes first in theory and then in a second paper through a clinical case report.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon  

The relationship between psychoanalysis and politics has always been a disputed one. On the one hand have been those, probably a majority, who see the two standing in distinct, if not opposing, spheres. On the other are those, certainly a significant number today, who find in psychoanalysis at least the possibility of a social critique (the ‘ambivalence of psychoanalysis’ identified by David Ingleby), if not the inherently subversive view of society found by others, notably Norman Brown and Russell Jacoby. For much of her life, the Austrian psychoanalyst Marie Langer lived the tension between psychoanalysis and politics, refusing to subordinate one to the other but seeking a praxis, a unity of theory and practice forged in activity.

Born into a middle-class (secular) Jewish family in Vienna in 1910, Marie Langer trained as a doctor, one of the first women to do so in Austria. She came to psychoanalysis through psychiatry and entered analysis with Richard Sterba (after Heinz Hartmann told her, rather condescendingly, that she probably could not afford his fees). This became her training analysis after Anna Freud accepted her at the Wiener Vereinigung. At the same time, Langer was an active member of the Austrian Communist Party which she had joined in response to the rise of the Nazis in Germany and the threat of Austro-fascism at home. The Party was declared illegal six weeks after Langer joined it, and its first clandestine congress was held in her flat. Later, Langer was to be called on to smuggle top Party functionaries out of Austria into Czechoslovakia.

Living with both her Communist activities and psychoanalysis was not easy. In 1934 the Vienna Institute of Psychoanalysis, in a misguided attempt to protect psychoanalysis from repression, laid down that no analyst could be active in a clandestine party or even treat someone who was. (By this time, the social democratic parties had also been banned in addition to the Communists and the far left.) Typically, Langer ignored the decree only to be given a stern warning when her continued political activity was discovered through a breach of analytic confidence.

Comment on Dr Donati's ‘A Psychodynamic Observer in a Chronic Psychiatric Ward’

R. Hinshelwood

R. Hinshelwood

R. Hinshelwood  

Work in a large and traditional Mental Hospital as a Consultant Psychotherapist provokes questions about the psychological adjustment of staff faced with the grim and often despairing tasks met within these institutions. When I first went to work in a large traditional Mental Hospital, one of my first impressions was surprise that people would be willing to work there. Many people had spent their whole careers in these institutions - institutions that had recently been publicly vilified in scandals and official enquiries (e.g. Inskip 1976).

I began to wonder how people coped. For myself, one way I coped was to approach it as a research problem worthy of investigation (Hinshelwood 1979).

The Mental Hospital appears to be an excellent opportunity to become familiar with the features of a demoralised institution. These include a sagging belief in the purpose and effectiveness of the institution. Often this is projected onto other groups within the institutions - like the administrators - ‘If it wasn't for them we would be able to get on without interference’; or the works department; or some other Aunt Sally. There is a retreat into cynical though often humorous stories about the parlous state of the institution. Individual members of staff seek a position for themselves and their own work or department, quite without reference to the needs of the institution's primary task. Personal empire building of this kind leads to considerable rivalry and bitterness as it is based on the attempt to secure a personal sense of work in an institution which cannot offer anybody a feeling of value or adequate job satisfaction. Such processes lead in the end to a fragmented institution with the parts working against each other, each one able to point to the uncooperativeness of someone else. A pernicious vicious circle develops that traps the institution into a permanently demoralised state.

Elizabeth Bott (1976) has described the peculiarly difficult task of the modern Mental Hospital to meet the conflicting needs of society - the needs of patients for asylum; the needs of society at large and the hospital staff in particular to believe in the benefits of treatment often forcefully administered; and the needs of families and others to incarcerate mad relatives in custodial safety. The incompatibility of these demands on the staff leads to persistent ‘job dissatisfaction’.

On the Integration of Cognitive-Behaviour Theory with Psychoanalysis

Peter Fonagy

Peter Fonagy

Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT

Peter Fonagy  

We are very far from the day when we will be able to specify the appropriate mixture of therapeutic approaches to be applied to a single patient (i.e. fitting the patient to the therapy). A commitment to eclectic or multi-modal psychotherapy is gaining ground within the discipline of psychotherapy (London 1972, Lazarus 1981, Goldfried 1982, Messer 1986). The mildest form that such integration may take is the differential therapy-oriented diagnosis of an individual patient. Implicitly the diagnostician conceives of certain patients as suffering from disorders which are oriented towards cognitive therapy whilst others have ‘deeper’ psychotherapeutically based problems. In this vein Murray (1976), for example, asserted that symptoms such as circumscribed phobias or specific sexual dysfunctions arise out of traumatic events and exist within a ‘sound personality structure’. Murray further claims that hysteria and obsessivecompulsive neurosis constitute disorders where symptoms are aspects of underlying personality disorder, ego functioning is fragile, inter-personal problems are prominent and an in-depth dynamic approach is more appropriate. Similiar suggestions have been made by Marks and Gelder (1966), Woody (1968), Marmor (1971), Bowers (1980) Messer and Winokur (1980, 1984, 1986). Ann Douglas' paper in the last issue of the Journal is a further example of this distinguished tradition.

One can well understand the motivation behind this approach, the wish of the clinician with integrity to help each patient with the most powerful technique conceivably applicable to the person's problems as formulated by the therapist. Most practising clinicians are forced by limitations of available facilities to make decisions about the type of therapy they regard as most likely to be of benefit to a particular patient. The difficulty of fitting the treatment to the patient is simply that, notwithstanding considerable empirical research devoted to this issue, no simple formula has been found which will indicate the appropriate treatment for a particular psychiatric or psychodynamic diagnosis. Early meta-analyses (quantitative reviews of large numbers of psychotherapy outcome studies) of controlled outcome studies (Smith et a11980) hinted that cognitive and dynamic therapy may be best applied to affective disorders whilst behaviour therapy is effective for phobic and obsessional states. Later meta-analytic studies (Shapiro & Shapiro 1982) found negligible interactions between problems and treatments. This is hardly surprising; if we examine Murray's admittedly simplistic formula its inadequacy quickly becomes manifest. Behaviour therapy, both cognitive and traditional, is surprisingly effective with disorders where considerable disintegration of personality functioning provides the backdrop to the symptomatic difficulties.

A Dictionary of Kleinian Thought by R.D. Hinshelwood. Published by Free Association Books1989; 482 pp.; £35 hardback.

Ronald Britton

Ronald Britton

Ronald Britton  

This is an ambitious enterprise and many will think it very necessary. Perhaps only a fellow analyst of the same school can fully appreciate how formidable an undertaking it is. To convey the sense and vitality of essentially clinically based concepts with a scholarly approach to their place in the history of psychoanalytic ideas is to demand rigour in two dimensions and in the main Bob Hinshelwood has succeeded. The term ‘Kleinian Thought’ suggests a degree of coherence and uniformity which does not really correspond to the reality of the ‘thoughts’ of Kleinian analysts who are more individualistic than most and who make a virtue of having a ‘loose end’ approach to analytic theory. They tend as a group to distrust systematic approaches to theory and to use certain basic concepts such as the ‘Depressive Position’ simply as organising ideas. As a result other theories and observations proliferate around these often in the personal language of individuals who do not always relate them to the usage of their closest colleagues. An exception to that will illustrate what I mean. Roger Money Kyrle wrote that his concept of ‘imageless expectations’ and Wilfred Bion's notion of ‘preconceptions’ was probably the same and his customary modesty led him to adopt Bion's usage. In other cases some concepts arrived at with great clinical perspicuity and rigour are linked in a vital way to their clinical context and how exactly they relate to a closely related theory may well remain problematical. I think an example of this is Segal's theory of ‘symbolic function’ and Bion's ‘theory of thinking’ which were developed at the same time by colleagues who shared a common approach and who felt they were saying similar things. Hanna Segal like all her successors has incorporated a great deal of Bion's thinking into her own and yet I do not think that his formulation covers the ground delineated by her own concept of ‘symbolic equations’. It has become common to equate these ‘symbolic equations’ (mental symbols treated by their producers as material objects) with Bion's notion of beta elements i.e. unprocessed raw data awaiting transformation into usable mental form by an unknown process he called alpha process. I think this is wrong and results from a wish to conflate rather different phenomena. Hinshelwood in one place appears to do this and yet his method of tracing the provenance of ideas and giving a proper account of them in their own right saves him from absorbing one theory into another, in an all too familiar way, to produce the appearance of linear development, which characterises some accounts of psychoanalytic theory, notably Guntrip's and Meltzer's.

Images of Freud by Barry Richards. Published by J.M. Dent, London 1989; 211 pages; £7. 95 paperback.

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

This book has an entrancing quality for the analyst or psychoanalytic psychotherapist. In this book Barry Richards writes less as a practitioner and more as a social scientist who is happily frank about the limited authority that this gives him to write about Freud. His interest is in the fate that Freud has met in our society.

He is not primarily concerned to expound what Freud really said, more what various people have said he said. And why Freud has been taken up in particular ways by particular people, in our particular world, at this particular moment in history. His thesis is that Freud's theories tend to be reconstructed to suit a particular outlook; as a generalised overview of his argument he states:

Market society has generated various forms of psychology which unwittingly and uncritically reflect both its utilitarian workings and its omnipotent phantasies about itself. It has also given rise to psychoanalysis as a contrary and reparative project, an attempt to renew our personal matrices of meaning amidst the amoral disorder of the market. At the same time psychoanalysis offers us ways of theorizing both the general psychic damage done by market relations and the specific illusions expressed in other psychological theories. (p. 146)

Firstly, he is interested in the historical variation in the popularity of Freud; for instance, psycho-analysis grew popular between the wars but fell back especially amongst professional psychologists and psychiatrists during the 1950's and 1960's due, he says, to the vogue for behaviourist psychology which described the external manifestations of the human being only. A turning point in cultural attitudes occurred in the 1960's from which psycho-analysis has fundamentally benefited. The political upheavals of 1968 were nothing short of a watershed in the political history of the twentieth century. Since then there has been an increasingly popular and intellectual demand for greater understanding of the interiority of human beings, which by definition behaviourism cannot supply.

Establishing boundaries is a dynamic process and it involves the way the (m)other is met as different. The Transformation Function in Light of a New Model of the Mind

Robert Langs MD

Robert Langs

408 Fierman Hall, 317 East 17th Street, New York 10003, USA

Robert Langs  

The paper introduces a new model of the mind based on psychoanalytic listening which attends carefully to the distinctions between derivative and nonderivative communication, and the three levels of meaning in messages - manifest, implication and encoded. The model forms a basis for revising Freud's theory of primary and secondary process thinking as well as notions of unconscious communication, experience and information processing.

The paper then conceptualises a particular subsystem of the model - the transformation subsystem (TSS). The transformation function safeguards processing which takes place in the deep unconscious system at a high level of perceptiveness and intelligence. The information processed is coated with anxiety and terror, and the transformation function assures that the images involved will not gain direct access to awareness. Displacement and symbolisation are the essential components of this processing system.

On this basis, patients are classified as transformers or nontransformers, and factors in this aspect of communicative style are presented. The basic flaw in the human mind to which the transformation function contributes, namely, that information derived from the processing which takes place in the deep unconscious system is not available for conscious adaptation, is identified and discussed. Nonetheless, the transformation function is seen as a safeguard against somatisation, acting out and, more fundamentally, as a modulating factor in the human psyche. The means by which the transformation function safeguards against symptom formation is articulated, as is the means by which the therapist may assist the patient in expressing him or herself in this fashion.

The paper concludes with a comparison between Bion's Alpha function theory and the present theory of transformations. Brief mention is made of the dysfunctions in the TSS in schizophrenic patients.

[[RunningHead]]

Penis Greed

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke

41 Weston Park, London N8

Joseph Berke  

Penis Greed is an insatiable desire for the male member and all the perks and privileges that seem to accompany it. Typically men feel: ‘… the bigger your cock, the more of a man you are’, while women declaim: ‘When one has it, one has everything, one feels protected, nothing can touch you’ (Penny 1981).

Such preoccupations extend from the anatomical organ to far-reaching concerns about strength, power, authority, virility, ambition, energy and enterprise, which account for Carl Jung's trenchant remark, ‘the penis is only a phallic symbol’ (Rycroft 1972).

The longing for male qualities, functions and status, ‘the phallus’, features in many cultures, but in this century Freud drew special attention to phallic wishes during the course of describing the development of female sexuality. He called the sudden shocking awareness of absent maleness and the wish to overcome it, ‘penis envy’. Related to the castration complex or the masculine complex, this term (and attendant assumptions) has achieved a prominent place in the psychological literature and popular parlance. But I believe it is a misnomer and, as generally used, perpetuates several misconceptions.

The classical concept of ‘penis envy’ has little to do with envy. On the contrary it conveys intense admiration, emulation and identification for all things masculine. It is a wish, first for a penis, then for a penis in intercourse, and finally for a penis substitute, such as, a baby.

An admixture of resentful, raging, spiteful, spoiling, begrudging, belittling attitudes and actions towards men, maleness and male organs certainly does exist. This is appropriately called penis envy and can be expressed by the penis as well as towards it. I shall soon discuss this complex in considerable detail but it was not an essential part of Freud's initial formulations.

The early analysts also believed that penis envy, or what I call penis greed, was essentially a biologically determined feature of females which condemns them to spend much of their life trying to regain something they had been born without. More succinctly, Freud stated: ‘Anatomy is destiny’ (1924). This epigram is based on one by Napoleon. He too spent much of his life trying to overcome an accident of birth. Certainly potency and power are not issues limited to the female sex. Most boys and men are obsessed with being bigger, stronger and more powerful than others, even if they have to conquer the world. This is an expression of the small penis complex or the Napoleon syndrome.

Trauma and its Aftermath

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

A conference on Trauma and Its Aftermath was held at Queen's College, Cambridge, on 6-8 April 1989 by the Royal College of Psychiatrists, Psychotherapy Section, Dr Jon Sklar and Dr Andrew Powell organised a rigorous schedule of papers, small group and large group discussions for 140 people.

There were six speakers, Dr Earl Hopper, Dr Brendan MacCarthy, Dr John Alderdice, Mrs Caroline Garland, Dr Hanna Segal and Dr Brian Martindale, who gave papers on different aspects of trauma. Dr Hopper opened the conference with a paper entitled Social Trauma and Psychotic Anxieties; Massification/Aggregation, Fusion/Fragmentation. It was a challenging paper, and in our small group discussions many of us tried to understand his concepts and how they applied; but as Dr Dennis Brown pointed out in the plenary, by the end of the conference we all knew from experience what he had been talking about. We had witnessed in the Large Group the pressure towards massification and the backing away from this, that takes place within groups and within ourselves.

The Friday morning started with Dr MacCarthy giving us a paper on Child Abuse, a Social, Family and Individual Trauma, in which he conveyed the multi-generational factors in child abuse. Paradoxically he left us with the feeling that though child abuse runs like a fissure through the psyche, in the hands of one as skilled as Dr MacCarthy, some healing can take place. This was followed by Dr Alderdice's paper on The Psychopathology and Politics of Aids. He read us passages from Camus' The Plague and brought home to us all how difficult it is to think about Aids. What are the facts? What are the implications? How easily we all, as Camus pointed out, feel that it cannot happen to us.

In the afternoon we were given a paper by Mrs Garland, External Disaster and the Internal World - Consultation work with Survivors, in which she was able to convey to us all something of the suffocating and terrifying experience of two survivors from a recent disaster. In some detail she suggested that the way each of these people dealt with the traumatic experience was intimately bound up with their internal world. At the moment of total helplessness the defence system broke down and earlier wounds were opened up again. The present experience seemed to have a psychic equivalence to earlier experiences so that earlier failures were felt to be repeating themselves. It might be said that we caught a glimpse of character being formed as Mrs Garland described the different ways in which these two survivors dealt with the disaster. We were left with a profound feeling of awe at the way these two people had managed. Her paper also threw up many questions which we discussed in our small groups: not least the question, what do we need in order to have the capacity to survive life threatening disasters?

What Happens in Groups. Psychoanalysis, the Individual and the Community by R.D. Hinshelwood. Published by Free Association Books, London, 1987; 278 pages; £9.95 paperback.

D. James

D. James

D. James  

In the closing paragraphs of this interesting book, the author quotes Bion as saying:

Characteristics in the individual whose real significance cannot be understood unless it is realized that they are part of his equipment as a herd animal and their operation cannot be seen unless it is looked for in the intelligible field of study - which in this instance is the group.…' (Bion 1961, p. 133)

Hinshelwood extends this by saying that no group exists without having the equipment for being a community and contributing to a system of sub-groups within a community.

He says: ‘In this sense the group and its individual cannot be understood unless the pieces of equipment for life as a community - especially dramatisations, barriers and bridging - are looked for’ (p. 263). By the time one arrives here, one has fully understood dramatisation, barriers and bridging since these are the terms used frequently by the author in his explorations of the inter-personal and group phenomena which he describes in the life of a therapeutic community.

Every psychotherapist should study this book, let alone every new psychiatric trainee or psychotherapy trainee of whatever discipline.

On first sight of the title, one might think, ‘Ah! at last someone is going to tell me!’ With this in mind, one might start reading the book and become initially disappointed and think that it is a book just about therapeutic communities; that would be a grave misunderstanding and misrepresentation of what the author has given us. Using his experience in a therapeutic community, he has built up, from the clinical to the theoretical, a much wider and more important view of the relationship between the individual and the group in which he functions and beyond that.

From his extensive clinical experince in the setting of the therapeutic community Hinshelwood, borrowing from Main (1977), is concerned with the ‘gel’ which makes some communities work while others are not so good. Main's ‘human folkways’ is an essential concept and he is at pains to understand and moreover be able to explain his understanding of this particular ingredient as part of the containing function.
